text:
Sec.  2-555.  Conduct of hearings.
(a)  The chairman of the board may call hearings of the  board.  Hearings  may  also  be  called  by  written notice,  signed  by  at  least  three  (3)  members  of  the board, or at the call of the city manager. The board, at a  hearing,  may set a future hearing date. The board shall adopt rules for the conduct of its hearings. Minutes shall be kept of all hearings and all hearings shall be open to the public. The city shall provide clerical and  administrative  personnel  as  may  be  reasonably required  for  the  proper  performance  of  the  board's duties.
(b)  The city attorney, or designee thereof, shall present evidence before the board on behalf of the city. If the alleged violator has been properly noticed in regard to the hearing before the board and fail to appear, the board may proceed with a hearing in absentia on the merits of the alleged violation. Any findings or orders resulting from such hearing are valid and binding upon the violator.
(c)  All parties shall have an opportunity to present evidence and argument on all issues involved, to conduct cross-examination and submit rebuttal evidence, and to be represented by counsel. When appropriate, the  general  public  may  be  given  an  opportunity  to present oral or written communications. If the agency
CD2:80
proposes  to  consider  such  material,  then  all  parties shall be given an opportunity to cross-examine or challenge or rebut it. The board may consider any evidence, including  evidence  of  the  general  reputation  of  the place or premises. All testimony shall be under oath and shall be recorded. Formal rules of  evidence shall not apply, but fundamental due process shall be observed and shall govern the proceedings. Orders of the board  shall  be  based  on  competent  and  substantial evidence.
(d)  After considering all evidence, the board may declare the place or premises to be a public nuisance and, if so, may immediately order any one (1) or all of the following:
(1) The discontinuance of the nuisance;
(2) The closing of the place or premises;
(3) The  prohibition  of  conduct,  operation,  or maintenance of any business or activity on the premises, and/or business or activity which is conducive  to  the  maintenance  of  such  nuisance;
(4) The payment to the city  by  the  operator  of fines  in  increments  of two  hundred  fifty ($250.00) dollars or another appropriate higher or lesser amount as it deems appropriate and necessary, per incident and/or day of noncompliance. In addition to such fines, the board may impose additional fines and/or assessed costs to cover all costs incurred by the city in investigation, remediation, enforcement, and prosecution of  violations enumerated herein, including attorney fees. Fines shall not exceed fifteen thousand dollars ($15,000.00) (or a total  amount  as  allowed  by  F .S.  §  893.138,  as amended) each time a premises is declared a public nuisance;
(5) The board may order the operator to provide additional  private  security  at  the  operator's sole expense, or such other reasonable remedial measures (including, but not limited to, lighting or fencing) as may be deemed effective to remedy or cure the public nuisance. If  the operator fails to take such action within the time specified by the board in its order, the city may take the action itself and seek to recover
ADMINISTRATION
any  expense  incurred  therein  by  any  lawful means, including the imposition of additional fines as set forth herein;
(6) The board may order any combination of subsection (d)(1) through (5) of this section.
(e)  All orders of  the board shall be by motion approved by a majority of  those members present and voting, except that at least three (3) members of  the board must vote in order for the action to be official.
(f)  An  order  entered  under  subsection  (d)  of  this section shall expire after one (1) year or at such earlier time  as  stated  in  the  order.  The  board  shall  retain jurisdiction to modify its orders or to extend the time period of  jurisdiction past the expiration date, upon the showing of cause that the operators have not taken reasonable and/or sufficient action to abate the public nuisance or there are additional public nuisance activities, or the operators have not adhered to the order of the board, prior to the expiration of said orders.
(g)  The  board  may  bring  a  complaint  under  F.S. § 60.05, seeking a temporary or permanent injunction against any public nuisance.
(Ord. No. 08-08, § 4, 7-9-2008)

text:
Sec.  2-556.  Recording  of  orders,  fines  and  costs;  enforcement of orders.
(a)  A certified copy of  an order declaring a premises  a  public  nuisance  and  other  orders  to  abate  the nuisance and imposing fines and/or costs or penalties assessed under section 2-555(d), may be recorded in the public  records  and,  thereafter,  shall  constitute  a  lien against the land on which the violation exists, or upon any other real or personal property owned by the violator  operator;  and  it  may  be  enforced  in  the  same manner as a court judgment by the sheriffs of this state, including levy against personal property, but shall not be deemed a court judgment except for enforcement purposes. Whenever a notice of complaint has resulted in a fine being levied or a board order, a copy of such final order shall be filed in the office of the clerk of the circuit court of the county who shall cause the same to be recorded among the public records of  the county. The  recordation  of  such  final  order  shall  constitute constructive notice to any subsequent purchasers, transferees, grantees, mortgagors, mortgagees, lessees, lienors, and all persons having, claiming or acquiring any interest in the premises described therein, or affected thereby. When  the  nuisance  specified  in  said  final  order  has
§ 2-556
been  abated  and  all  fines  and  costs  for  enforcement have been paid, a certificate certifying the nuisance has been abated shall be filed and the order cancelled. All such final orders shall include the proper legal description of  the premises involved. The costs of  recording the original final order and the certificate of cancellation shall also be recoverable as costs from the operator prior to recording the certificate of  cancellation. The original final order may include an automatic date of cancellation/expiration, exclusive of the costs/fines liens, and shall be effective if the board has not filed a notice of  extension  as  allowed  under  section  2-555(f).  Any person  acquiring  any  interest  in  or  to  property  described in a final order after recordation thereof, shall take the property subject to the requirements set forth in  the  final  order,  and  all  other  provisions  of  this article. After the filing of any such lien which remains unpaid, the city attorney's office may foreclose or otherwise execute on the lien. Interest shall accrue on the unpaid costs and/or fines at the annual interest rate of eighteen (18) percent. No lien created pursuant to the provisions herein may be foreclosed on real property, which is a homestead under section 4, article X of the state constitution.
(b)  In addition to the enforcement remedies available to the city in subsection (a) of this section, the city attorney may initiate contempt proceedings in the circuit  court  of  the  county  for  willful  disobedience  or failure to comply with any order of the board. The city attorney is also further authorized to initiate proceedings  in  any  county,  state,  or  federal  forum  for  the suspension or revocation of any permits, licenses, concessions, or contracts held or awarded to the violator operator,  including  contracts  awarded  under  F.S. § 24.112, and including licenses for the sale of  beverages issued under F.S. § 561.19, where the existence of such permits, licenses, concessions or contracts is conducive to the maintenance of such public nuisance.
(c)  An order of  the board issued pursuant to this article  shall  also  be  posted  at  the  place,  building,  or premises where the public nuisance exists, existed or is occurring, in violation of the law and shall be sent by certified  mail  to  the  owner  of  record  of  such  place, building, or premises within two (2) business days of the posting.
(d)  City  police  officers  shall  be  authorized  to  act upon and enforce such orders in accordance with section 2-555, five (5) business days after the posting of an order issued pursuant to the board.

(e)  Any  operator,  or  person  who  hinders,  or  obstructs,  any  state,  county,  or  city  official,  in  the  discharge of his duties under this article, or in carrying out the  orders  of  the  board,  or  who  fails  to  follow  the orders of the board, shall be cited by the police department, and upon conviction thereof in the county court, shall be punished by a fine not to exceed five hundred dollars ($500.00) or by imprisonment in the county jail for not more than sixty (60) days, or by both such fine and imprisonment.
(f)  In  the  event  the  board  orders  the  operator  to close the premises and/or secure it, and the operator fails to do so, as determined by city officials, or other county or state agencies, the city shall be authorized to secure the premises as necessary to safeguard the public health, safety, and welfare. The operator will automatically be assessed the costs and be subject to lien and foreclosure action as in subsection (a) of this section.
(g)  When any nuisance, as defined in F.S. § 823.05, exists, the city attorney, or any resident or visitor to the city, may sue in the name of the state on his relation to enjoin the public nuisance, the person maintaining it, and the owner or agent of  the premises on which the public nuisance exists.
(Ord. No. 08-08, § 5, 7-9-2008)

Sec.  2-556.1.  Appeals.
An aggrieved party, including the city administration,  may  appeal  a  final  administrative  order  of  the housing  authority  and  nuisance  abatement  board  to the Circuit Court of the Eleventh Judicial Circuit. An appeal shall be filed within thirty (30) days  of  the  date  of  rendition  of  the  written  order appealed from.
(Ord. No. 08-08, § 6, 7-9-2008)

Sec.  2-570.26.  Jurisdiction.
(a)  The city code enforcement special magistrates appointed by the city commission shall have jurisdiction to hear and decide cases in which violations are alleged of any provisions of technical codes enacted by the city, including, but not limited to, property standards, business tax, fire, building, zoning and sign code, as  well  as  the  Florida  Building  Code,  Miami-Dade County Edition.
(b)  Where there is more than one (1) special magistrate, cases will be assigned by lot.
(c)  Any alleged violation of the aforesaid codes and ordinances may also be enforced in any court of competent jurisdiction.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.26; Ord. No. 97-1, § 1, 1-22-1997)

The  city  commission  shall  appoint  no  more  than three (3) preapproved special magistrates and an alternate. Sec.  2-570.29.  Definitions.
The following words, terms and phrases, when used in  this  division,  shall  have  the  meanings  ascribed  to them in this section, except where the context clearly indicates a different meaning:
Applicant means a property owner, tenant or someone who is substantially  affected  by  an  enforcement action or developmental order.
City means the City of Opa-locka, Florida.
Clerk or clerk of code enforcement means the administrative  staff  person  in  the  city's  code  enforcement division responsible for the preparation, development
§ 2-570.29
and coordination of all administrative and case management services necessary for the proper administration of the special magistrate proceedings.
Code means any of the several chapters of the Code of Ordinances or zoning and development regulations of the city or the Florida Building Code, Miami-Dade County Edition, as described in section 2-570.26.
Code  enforcement  officer or code  inspector means any designated employee or agent of  the city whose duty it is to enforce codes and ordinances enacted by the city. There are hereby designated certain employees and agents of the city as code enforcement officers for the purposes of this article. Employees or agents hereby designated  as  code  enforcement  officers  include,  but are not limited to, building inspectors, building official, code enforcement officers, and police officers  of  the city. Code enforcement officers, as defined herein, shall have the authority to issue a citation to a person when, based  upon  investigation,  the  officer  has  reasonable cause to believe that the person has committed a civil infraction in violation of a duly enacted code or ordinance  and  that  the  special  magistrate  will  hear  the charge.
Final  order means  an  order  issued  by  the  special magistrate. Such orders shall have the force of  law to command whatever steps are necessary to bring a violation into compliance.
Participant means:
(a) A person holding title to land contiguous to the owner's property, who has been accepted by the special magistrate as a participant in the proceeding; or
(b) A substantially affected person who submitted oral or written testimony, sworn or unsworn, on a substantive nature which stated with particularly support for or objections to the code enforcement action or order in a prior proceeding, including a public hearing, and who has been accepted by the special magistrate as a participant in the proceeding.
Party includes the owner, the city, and any governmental entity made a party to the proceeding by the special magistrate upon application of  the owner, the city or any other governmental activity.

§ 2-570.29
OPA-LOCKA CODE
Probable cause means a reasonable belief that code provisions has been violated and that the violator committed or is the person responsible for maintaining the violation.
Quasi-judicial proceeding means a nonlegislative proceeding wherein the mayor, commissioners and/or board or agency members are required to ascertain the existence of  facts  and  draw conclusions from them as a basis for their respective official action. Quasi-judicial proceedings refer only to variances, special exceptions, development approvals that require subsequent court approval and certain permit and license decisions, including extended hours licenses and distance waivers under the city's zoning and land development regulations  to  be  made  by  the  city  commission,  as  well  as those quasi-judicial decisions made by city administrative boards and agencies, including the special magistrates,  planning  and  zoning  board,  personnel  board and housing authority. Ex parte communications on quasi-judicial proceedings are prohibited.
Recommended order means an order issued by the special magistrate after notice and an opportunity to be heard at a public hearing has been afforded to the complaining property owner who believes that his/her private  property  rights  have  been  inordinately  burdened, restricted,  or  limited  due  to  laws,  regulations and ordinances. The recommended order shall be submitted to the city commission for its acceptance, rejection  or  modifications  and  shall  become  final  upon approval, in accordance with F.S. ch. 70.
Repeat violation means a violation of a provision of a  code  or  ordinance  by  a  person  whom  the  special magistrate previously found to have violated the same provision  within  five  (5)  years  prior  to  the  current violation.
Special magistrate means any person who is a member in good standing of  the Florida Bar and who is appointed by the city commission to serve as a special magistrate under this chapter.
Violator means any property owner, tenant or business entity on the premises, or any combination thereof, and each notice shall so state.

Sec.  2-570.30.  Citation  and  enforcement  procedures; supplemental.
(a)  It  shall  be  the  duty  of  the  code  enforcement officer to initiate enforcement proceedings of the various  codes  or  ordinances;  however,  no  member  of  a board shall have the power to initiate such enforcement proceedings.
(b)  A citation issued by a code enforcement officer shall  be  as  provided  by  state  law.  Prior  to  issuing  a citation,  a  code  enforcement  officer  shall  provide  a courtesy notice to the person that the person has committed a violation of a code or applicable law and shall have (5) days within which said violation is to be corrected. If  the violation has not been corrected within five (5) days, the code enforcement officer shall issue a citation to the person who has committed the violation.
(c)  A  person  who receives a citation from a code enforcement  officer  for  the  violation  of  a  city  ordinance  has  committed  a  civil  infraction  and  shall  be subject to a fine in accordance with the schedule of civil penalties under section 2-570.33.
(d)  After issuing a citation to an alleged violator, a code enforcement officer shall deposit the original citation and one (1) copy of the citation with the special magistrate.
(e)  Nothing contained in this chapter shall prohibit the  city  from  enforcing  its  ordinances  by  any  other means.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.30; Ord. No. 97-1, § 1, 1-22-1997; Ord. No. 03-26, § 2, 10-8-2003)

text:
Sec.  2-570.31.  Hearing procedures before special magistrate.
(a) Date of hearing.
Written notice means the mailing of notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, or by hand delivery, to the person required to be notified for an alleged code violation thereby advising the alleged violator of  the date, time and location for any hearing on the alleged
CD2:84
(1) A  time  and  date  for  the  special  magistrate hearing shall be set and noticed in accordance with the provisions below. The violator may file a written reply to the charges contained in the notice of violations which shall be known as "the response." The response must contain
ADMINISTRATION
the  address  of  the  violation  and  the  alleged violator's relationship to the property (for example: owner, tenant, and the like).
(2) At the time and place set for the hearing, the special magistrate shall hear and consider all testimony  allowable  and  shall  examine  and consider  all  the  relevant  evidence  presented. After the conclusion of  the hearing, the special magistrate shall issue findings of fact and conclusions  of  law  in  a  written  final  order affording the proper relief consistent with the powers granted herein. Such order may command a violator to take whatever steps necessary to bring a violation into compliance by the time announced at the hearing and subsequently placed in the order. The findings, conclusions and final order of the special magistrate shall be announced orally at the special magistrate  hearing  and  shall  be  reduced  to writing and mailed to the violator.
(b) Enforcement and notice requirements.
(1) If  a violation of a code is alleged to exist, the code enforcement officer shall, unless subsection (b)(2) of this section applies, provide written notice to the alleged violator of the violation and afford that person a reasonable time, in light of the nature of the violation, to correct it. Should the violation continue beyond the time specified for correction, the code enforcement officer shall notify the clerk, who shall schedule a hearing before a special magistrate; and the officer, clerk, law enforcement officer, or other person designated by the city shall provide written notice by hand delivery or certified mail, return receipt requested, to the  alleged  violator  of  the  hearing.  At  the option of  the special magistrate, notice may additionally be served by publication or posting.
(2) If a repeat violation is found, the code enforcement officer shall notify the violator but is not required to give the violator a reasonable time to correct the violation. The code enforcement officer, upon notifying the violator of a repeat violation, shall notify the clerk of code enforcement and request a hearing. The code enforcement division, through its clerical staff, shall schedule  a  hearing  and  shall  provide  notice
CD2:85
§ 2-570.31
pursuant to subsection (b)(1) of  this section. The case may be presented to the special magistrate  even  if  the  repeat  violation  has  been corrected  prior  the  hearing,  and  the  notice shall so state.
(3) If  the code enforcement officer has reason to believe a violation or the condition causing the violation presents a serious threat to the public health, safety, and welfare or if the violation is irreparable or irreversible in nature, the code enforcement officer  shall  make  a  reasonable effort to notify the violator and may immediately notify the code enforcement division and request a hearing.
(c) Hearing procedures.
(1) No special magistrate shall act in any case in which that special magistrate has a conflict of interest. If the special magistrate has a conflict of  interest with any case, s/he shall orally announce such at the scheduled hearing, unless s/he  is  aware  of  such  conflict  prior  to  the hearing and shall notify the clerk of code enforcement, whereby that case shall be rescheduled for a hearing before another special magistrate.
(2) All hearings of the special magistrate shall be open  to  the  public,  and  any  person  whose interests may be affected by the matter before the special magistrate shall be given the opportunity to be heard. The record of all hearings, agendas, findings, determinations and final orders shall be maintained by the clerk of code enforcement.
(3) Hearings shall be informal and need not be conducted according to technical rules relating to evidence and witnesses. They shall, however,  be  conducted  in  accordance  with  accepted  parliamentary  procedures  relative  to motions,  votes  and  decisions.  Fundamental due process shall be observed and shall govern all hearings.
(4) All relevant evidence shall be admitted if, in the opinion of the special magistrate, it is the type of  evidence upon which reasonable and responsible persons would normally rely in the conduct of  business affairs, regardless of  the existence of any common law or statutory rule
§ 2-570.31
OPA-LOCKA CODE
which might make such evidence inadmissable over objections in civil action. The special magistrate may exclude irrelevant or unduly repetitious evidence.
(5) Hearsay evidence may be accepted for the purpose of  supplementing or explaining any direct evidence, but such hearsay evidence shall not in and of itself be considered sufficient to support a finding or decision unless the evidence would be admissible over objections in a civil action.
(6) Each party to the hearing shall have the right to call and examine witnesses, introduce exhibits,  cross-examine  opposing  witnesses,  impeach witnesses and rebut evidence.
(7) The alleged violator has the right, at his own expense, to be represented by an attorney at any special magistrate hearing.
(8) All testimony before the special magistrate shall be under oath and shall be recorded. The alleged violator or the city may cause the proceedings  to  be  recorded  by  a  certified  court reporter  or  by  a  certified  recording  instrument.
(9) The burden of  proof  shall be with the code inspector or code enforcement officer to show by the greater weight of evidence that a code violation exists and that the alleged violator committed, or was responsible for maintaining, the violation.
(10) If  written notice has been provided to an alleged violator of the hearing, a hearing may be conducted, and a final order rendered in the absence of the violator.
(11) The  special  magistrate  may,  for  good  cause shown, postpone or continue a hearing.
(d) City's option. Any alleged violation of the aforesaid codes and ordinances may also be enforced in any court of competent jurisdiction pursuant to the applicable notice provisions.
(e) Appeal process. An aggrieved party under these provisions  may  appeal  a  final  order  entered  by  the special magistrate to the circuit court within thirty (30) days of  its rendition. Failure to timely appeal a final order shall result in a waiver of all appeal rights.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.31; Ord. No. 97-1, § 1, 1-22-1997)

(11) The  special  magistrate  may,  for  good  cause shown, postpone or continue a hearing.
(d) City's option. Any alleged violation of the aforesaid codes and ordinances may also be enforced in any court of competent jurisdiction pursuant to the applicable notice provisions.
(e) Appeal process. An aggrieved party under these provisions  may  appeal  a  final  order  entered  by  the special magistrate to the circuit court within thirty (30) days of  its rendition. Failure to timely appeal a final order shall result in a waiver of all appeal rights.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.31; Ord. No. 97-1, § 1, 1-22-1997)

Sec.  2-570.32.  Conduct of hearing.
(a)  The special magistrate may call hearings. At any hearing, the special magistrate may set a future hearing date. Minutes shall be kept of all hearings by the special magistrate and all hearings and proceedings shall be open to the public. The city commission, by and through the city manager, shall provide necessary clerical and administrative  personnel  as  may  be  reasonably  required by the special magistrate for the proper performance of his duties.
(b)  Each case before the special magistrate shall be presented by either the city attorney, or an assistant to the city attorney, or an assistant city attorney, or by a member of the administrative staff of the city.
(c)  The special magistrate shall proceed to hear the cases on the agenda for that day. All testimony shall be under oath and shall be recorded. The special magistrate  shall  take  testimony  from  the  code  inspector/ officer and alleged violator. Formal rules of  evidence shall not apply but fundamental due process shall be observed and govern said proceedings.
(d)  At  the  conclusion  of  the  hearing,  the  special magistrate shall issue findings of fact, based upon the evidence  and  conclusions  of  law  and  shall  issue  an order  affording  the  proper  relief  consistent  with  the powers granted herein.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.32; Ord. No. 97-1, § 1, 1-22-1997)

text:
Sec.  2-570.44.  General provisions.
(a) Legislative  intent. The  proceeding  under  this section was established by the Florida Legislature in 1995  (F.S.  §  70.51)  to  provide  a  speedy,  inexpensive, simple, solution-oriented, nonjudicial method for settlement of  private property disputes. It is strictly voluntary for the private property owner; however, a governmental entity must participate if the private property owner files a request for relief. As much as possible, a landowner and governmental entity should meet faceto-face and seek a negotiated settlement of  the issue without the need for advocacy by a lawyer. If a settlement is not reached, the special magistrate conducts an independent and impartial assessment of  the dispute and prepares a nonbinding determination of whether the action by the government entity or entities is unreasonable or unfairly burdens the real property. If there is a determination of an unfair burden, the special magistrate with the owner's consent may recommend one (1) or more alternatives that protect the public interest and reduce restrictions on the use of the property.
CD2:88
(b) Preinitiation  meeting. Prior  to  filing  a  formal special magistrate proceeding under this subdivision, the owner may by letter request an informal meeting with  the  city  manager  or  his/her  designee  to  discuss alternatives to the filing of the special magistrate proceeding under this division. The city manager or his/ her designee shall conduct such a meeting as expeditiously  as  possible  and  shall  include  technical  staff familiar with the regulation/code section at issue.

(2) In order to initiate a special magistrate proceeding, an owner must file two (2) copies of a request for relief in the office of the city manager. The request for relief must be filed within thirty (30) days after receipt of  the order or notice of the city's action.
(3) The request for relief shall contain the following:
a. A  brief  statement  of  the  owner's  proposed use of the property.
ADMINISTRATION
b. A summary of the development order or description of the enforcement action. A copy of the development order or documentation  enforcement  action  at  issue must be attached to the request.
(4) Within ten (10) days of receipt of the request for relief, the city manager or his/her designee shall forward the request to a special magistrate selected from the preapproved list of special magistrates. This time period may be extended by agreement of the parties.
(5) The city shall include in the request for relief form provided to the property owner a list of preapproved special magistrates and instructions for objecting to any person named on the list. Unless a property owner objects to a special magistrate in the property owner's request for relief, the city will presume that all of  the listed special magistrates are mutually acceptable to the property owner, and the city will select one (1) of them as the special magistrate to consider the request for relief.
(6) If  the  property  owner  objects  to  all  of  the persons on the preapproved special magistrate list, the city shall be allowed additional time to secure  a  mutually  acceptable  special  magistrate.
(7) The cost of preparing and filing the initial two (2)  copies  of  the  request  for  relief  shall  be borne by the property owner or tenant and, the cost of preparing and serving copies of the request  for  relief  on  qualifying  participants, shall be borne equally by the parties.
(d) Notice of filing. Concurrently with the forwarding of  the request for relief  to the special magistrate, the city shall serve, U.S. mail or hand-delivery, a copy of the request to: (a) owners of real property contiguous to the applicant's property at the address shown on the  latest  county  tax  roll;  and  (b)  any  substantially affected  person  who  submitted  oral  or  written  testimony of a substantive nature which stated with particularity an objection to or support for any development order or enforcement action at issue. Notice to a substantially affected person is required only if that person indicated to the city a desire to receive notice of  any subsequent  special  magistrate  proceedings  occurring on the development order or enforcement action.
§ 2-570.44
(e) Filing of  response. Within fifteen (15) days following the filing of a request for relief with the city, the city manager or his/her designee shall file a response to the  request  for  relief  with  the  special  magistrate,  together  with  a  copy  to  the  applicant,  setting  forth  in reasonable detail the position of the city regarding the matters alleged by the applicant and including a brief statement explaining the public purpose of the regulations on which the development order or enforcement action is based. Any other government entity that is added by the special magistrate as a party must file a response prior to the hearing, but not later than fifteen (15) days following its admission as a party.
The city's response shall also include a sufficiency report which indicates whether the claim for relief contains the following information:
(1) A  brief  statement  of  the  owner's  proposed use of the property.
(2) A summary of the development order or description of the enforcement action. A copy  of  the  development  order  or  the documentation  of  an  enforcement  action  at  issue  must  be  attached  to  the request.
(3) A brief  statement of  the impact of  the development  order  or  enforcement  action on the ability of the owner to achieve the proposed use of the property.
(4) A certificate of service showing the parties,  including the governmental entity, served.
The cost of preparing and filing of the response to the request for relief shall be borne by the city.
(f) Sufficiency hearing. Prior to any hearing on the merits of  the request for relief, the special magistrate may conduct a hearing on whether the request for relief should be dismissed for failing to include the information required above. If the special magistrate dismisses the case, he or she shall allow the owner to amend the request and refile. The applicant and all parties in the matter shall receive a fifteen (15) day notice by U.S. mail  or  hand  delivery  regarding  the  date,  time  and location  of  the  sufficiency  hearing.  The  applicant's failure to submit an adequate amended request within the time specified by the special magistrate shall result in a dismissal with prejudice of the proceeding.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.44; Ord. No. 97-1, § 1, 1-22-1997)

Sec.  2-570.47.  Hearing procedures.
(a)  See  section  2-570.28  for  the  appointment  of preapproved special magistrates.
(b)  The city shall include the request for relief form provided to the owner a preapproved list of magistrates and instructions for objection to any person named on the list. The parties may mutually agree on a special magistrate.
(c)  Selection from the preapproved listing (applicable only for matters brought pursuant to the provisions under section 2-570.44 et al, i.e., Private Property Rights Act).
(1) The special magistrate may be selected from the list of preapproved special magistrates provided with the request for relief form. Unless a property owner or tenant objects to a special magistrate in the property owner's or tenant's request for relief, those special magistrates not objected to are deemed to be acceptable to the property owner or tenant. The city will select one  (1)  of  them,  at  random,  as  the  special magistrate to consider the request for relief.
(2) If  the property owner or tenant objects to all of the persons on the preapproved special magistrate list, the city shall assign the matter to a special magistrate on its list unless the objections reasonably show a conflict of interest.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.45; Ord. No. 97-1, § 1, 1-22-1997)

text:
Sec.  2-570.46.  Conduct of hearing.
(a)  In all respects, the hearing shall be informal and open to the public. The hearing shall operate at the direction and under the supervision of the special magistrate. The object of  the hearing is to focus attention on the impact of the governmental action giving rise to the request and to explore alternatives for relief.
(b)  The special magistrate shall act as a facilitator or mediator between the parties in an effort to effect a mutually acceptable solution. If an acceptable solution is not reached through the special magistrate's attempt at mediation, the special magistrate shall consider the facts and circumstances set forth in the request and any responses and any other information produced at the hearing in order to determine whether the action by the government entities  is  unreasonable  or  unfairly  burdens the real property.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.46; Ord. No. 97-1, § 1, 1-22-1997)
(a)  Hearings before the special magistrate shall be held  as  necessary  to  comply  with  state  law.  To  the maximum extent practicable, the hearings shall be informal.  Questioning  shall  be  confined  as  closely  as possible to the scope of  direct testimony. The special magistrate  may  call  and  question  witnesses  as  s/he deems necessary and appropriate. The special magistrate shall decide all questions of  procedure. The special  magistrate's  recommendation  is  a  public  record under F.S. ch. 119.
(b)  The  participants  before  the  special  magistrate shall be: (a) the applicant and witnesses; (b) city and other governmental representatives and witnesses; and (c) public and witnesses as provided by state law. Each participant shall be limited to a total of one (1) hour to present its case, provided that for good cause shown, the special magistrate may grant additional time.
(c)  The order of presentation at the hearing shall be as follows:
(1) Applicant and witnesses;
(2) The  city  manager's  response  to  the  application, including staff and other appropriate witnesses, as necessary;
(3) Other  governmental  participants  and  witnesses;
(4) Amended response  of  city  manager,  if  any; and
(5) Rebuttal and summation of applicant.
(d)  Any  part  of  the  evidence  may  be  received  in written form, and all testimony shall be under oath. The hearing shall be recorded, and minutes shall be kept. Hearsay evidence may be used for the purpose of supplementing or explaining other evidence, but it shall not be sufficient, in itself, to support a finding by the special magistrate unless it would be admissible over objections in a civil action.
(e)  At the discretion of the special magistrate, reasonable cross-examination of witnesses shall be permitted,  but  questioning  shall  be  confined  as  closely  as possible to the scope of direct testimony.
CD2:90
ADMINISTRATION
(f)  It shall be the duty of  the special magistrate to inquire fully into the facts of each case. In addition to the power described above, the special magistrate shall have the following powers and duties with respect to such cases:
(1) To  receive  stipulations  of  fact,  agreed  to  in writing, by the participants. Such stipulations, if filed, shall be regarded and used as evidence at  such  public  hearing.  A  special  magistrate may, nevertheless, require such additional evidence as he may deem necessary. However, a special magistrate shall not become an advocate for any participant in any zoning case, nor shall a special magistrate impose his/her theory of  the case upon any participant during the hearing.
(2) To accept, in lieu of  originals, true copies of such documentary evidence as may be offered.
(3) To request printed or written briefs to be filed on behalf  of  any of  the participants in such hearings. Such briefs shall contain an abstract of the evidence, and also the arguments relied on by the participant filing the same. Briefs, when requested,  shall  be  prepared  and  filed with the special magistrate within such time or times, and under such regulations, as to service of copies thereof upon the other participants, as the special magistrate may prescribe. The above-described request shall be filed on forms available from the code enforcement office or the city manager's office.
(4) To dispose of  procedural requests or similar matters including motions to modify and motions to consolidate applications.
(5) To call, examine and cross-examine witnesses and to introduce into the record all relevant evidence.
(6) To  keep  a  record  of  all  persons  requesting notice of the decision in each case.
(7) To receive oral testimony presented by all interested individuals.
(8) To exclude all irrelevant, immaterial and repetitive testimony and evidence.
CD2:91
§ 2-570.47
(9) To subpoena any nonparty witness in the city or state whom the special magistrate believes will aid in the disposition of  the request for relief.
(10) To visit the property which is the subject matter of the application.
(g)  The  special  magistrate  may  call  and  question witnesses as s/he deems necessary and appropriate.
(h)  The special magistrate shall decide all questions of procedure.
(i)  In conducting the hearing, the special magistrate may hear from all parties and witnesses that are necessary to an understanding of the matter and shall weigh all information offered at the hearing.
(j)  The  special  magistrate's  expenses  in  providing notice shall be borne equally by the parties or as otherwise  established  in  the  special  magistrate's  agreement.
(k)  At any time during the special magistrate proceeding a party may submit an offer to compromise.
(l)  At any time during the special magistrate proceeding, the owner and the city may enter into a settlement agreement or other agreement as to the permissible use of the owner's land.
(m)  A settlement agreement or other agreement as to  the  permissible  use  of  the  owner's  land  may  be executed by the parties involved. Any settlement agreement requiring the expenditure of funds, or the acquisition  of  funds,  a  variance  or  special  exemption  or other public hearing shall not be binding on any party until approved by all parties and the city commission.
(n)  The following forms of relief are available:
(1) Without limitation, relief may be in the form of  exemptions or variances from the applicable ordinances, including the city's comprehensive plan and other land development regulations;
(2) Relief may be conditional in nature. Such conditional relief  must be analyzed to determine if the conditions under which it is granted are consistent with the purpose and intent of the subject regulations and the city's comprehensive plan;
§ 2-570.47
OPA-LOCKA CODE
(3) Conditions may be initial, after satisfaction of which the settlement is implemented; or
(4) Conditions  may  be  ongoing,  the  failure  of which serve to vacate the settlement and divest the owner or his/her successors in interest of any right thereunder.
(o)  Any relief granted shall address the appropriateness of relief, allowing the city to fashion that form of relief necessary to equitably address the legitimate concerns  of  the  property  owner  while  at  the  same  time protecting the legitimate interests of the citizens of the city.  Such  decisions  shall  be  guided  by  the  criteria established in the Florida Land Use and Environmental Dispute Resolution Act under F.S. ch. 70.
(p)  Where such settlement or other agreement has been entered into, the special magistrate shall not thereafter render a recommendation on those matters covered by the agreement.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.47; Ord. No. 97-1, § 1, 1-22-1997)

(j)  The  special  magistrate's  expenses  in  providing notice shall be borne equally by the parties or as otherwise  established  in  the  special  magistrate's  agreement.
(k)  At any time during the special magistrate proceeding a party may submit an offer to compromise.
(l)  At any time during the special magistrate proceeding, the owner and the city may enter into a settlement agreement or other agreement as to the permissible use of the owner's land.
(m)  A settlement agreement or other agreement as to  the  permissible  use  of  the  owner's  land  may  be executed by the parties involved. Any settlement agreement requiring the expenditure of funds, or the acquisition  of  funds,  a  variance  or  special  exemption  or other public hearing shall not be binding on any party until approved by all parties and the city commission.
(n)  The following forms of relief are available:
(1) Without limitation, relief may be in the form of  exemptions or variances from the applicable ordinances, including the city's comprehensive plan and other land development regulations;
(2) Relief may be conditional in nature. Such conditional relief  must be analyzed to determine if the conditions under which it is granted are consistent with the purpose and intent of the subject regulations and the city's comprehensive plan;
§ 2-570.47
OPA-LOCKA CODE
(3) Conditions may be initial, after satisfaction of which the settlement is implemented; or
(4) Conditions  may  be  ongoing,  the  failure  of which serve to vacate the settlement and divest the owner or his/her successors in interest of any right thereunder.
(o)  Any relief granted shall address the appropriateness of relief, allowing the city to fashion that form of relief necessary to equitably address the legitimate concerns  of  the  property  owner  while  at  the  same  time protecting the legitimate interests of the citizens of the city.  Such  decisions  shall  be  guided  by  the  criteria established in the Florida Land Use and Environmental Dispute Resolution Act under F.S. ch. 70.
(p)  Where such settlement or other agreement has been entered into, the special magistrate shall not thereafter render a recommendation on those matters covered by the agreement.

text:
Sec.  2-570.48.  Special magistrate recommendation.
The special magistrate shall prepare a recommendation within fourteen (14) days of concluding hearings. The special magistrate shall send a copy of the recommendation in each case to all parties involved in the dispute. The special magistrate may recommend one (1) or more of the following alternatives, but shall not be limited to these alternatives:
(1) An adjustment of land development or permit standards or other provisions controlling the development or use of land.
(2) Increases or modifications in the density, intensity, or use of areas of development.
(3) The transfer of development rights.
(4) Land swaps or exchanges.
(5) Mitigation, including payments in lieu of onsite mitigation.
(6) Location on the least sensitive portion of the property.
(7) Conditioning the amount of  development or use permitted.
(9) Issuance of the development order, a variance, special exception, or other extraordinary relief, including withdrawal of the enforcement action.
(10) Purchase of  the real property, or an interest therein, by the city or other appropriate governmental entity.
(11) That  the  city  or  other  governmental  entity involved in the dispute maintain its position as valid.
(12) Assess fines, penalties and late fees for Code violations.
(13) Order cleanup or removal of Code violations.
(14) Issue stop orders on work done to property in violation of Code.
(15) Order any other legal method of  compliance with city Code.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.48; Ord. No. 97-1, § 1, 1-22-1997)

Sec.  2-570.49.  Response to special magistrate's recommendation.
The city, in consultation with other governmental entities participating in the proceeding, must respond to the special magistrate's recommendation within fortyfive (45) days by taking one (1) of the following actions:
(a) Accept the recommendation of the special magistrate as submitted and proceed to implement it by development agreement, when appropriate, or by other method, in the ordinary course and consistent with the rules and procedures of  the  city.  The  city  commission  may,  at  a public hearing, grant the necessary variances, special exceptions to the application or statutes, rules, regulations, or ordinances without the  need  for  such  items  going  to  any  other board or committee of  the city based on the recommendation  of  the  special  magistrate. However, an owner is not required to duplicate previous  processes  in  which  the  owner  has participated in order to effectuate the granting of the modification, variance, or special exception;

text:
Sec.  2-570.69.  Objectives.
The accountability board will provide standardized procedures for the city to ensure the uniform and effective handling of allegations of sexual harassment and other misconduct which may contribute to an offensive,  hostile  or  intimidating  work  environment.  The

accountability board will oversee the processing of allegations of  sexual harassment and other misconduct to ensure that they are responded to in a manner that is fair to all parties, timely, and consistent. The accountability board's oversight will provide the city with an assessment of the processing of allegations covered by this division, independent of  the officials responsible for such processing. The accountability board will review actions taken for timeliness, consistency, and appropriateness. The accountability board will not recommend or take disciplinary action. Benefits resulting from a process emphasizing accountability, timeliness, consistency, and appropriateness include:
(1) Ensuring  that  allegations  of  sexual  harassment and other misconduct which may contribute to an offensive, hostile or intimidating work environment are handled properly.
(2) Ensuring a uniform and consistent approach to address and track allegations.
(3) Creating and maintaining a model work environment to enhance mission accomplishment.
(4) Demonstrating the city's commitment to eliminate sexual harassment from the workplace.
(5) Potentially  reducing  the  expenditure  of  resources required by more formal procedures, such as equal employment opportunity (EEO) and reducing financial liability.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.69; Ord. No. 01-2, § 4, 2-14-2001)

text:
Sec.  2-570.70.  Timeliness standards.
Each  allegation  of  sexual  harassment  and  other misconduct which may contribute to an offensive, hostile  or  intimidating  work  environment  should  be  reported as soon as possible after the incident occurs. There is no specific time requirement for employees to report  instances  of  sexual  harassment  under  the  accountability board process. However, the city's ability to deal with such issues appropriately and effectively, particularly when disciplinary action is warranted, is greatly diminished if  the allegations are not reported timely. Accordingly, employees are encouraged to report  such  incidents  promptly.  The  goal  is  that  such allegations will be reported to the accountability board and, if  appropriate, investigated and appropriate action initiated within a total of fifty (50) workdays from the date the allegation was reported. Specific timeframes for various stages of the process are provided for in this

Sec.  2-570.70.  Timeliness standards.
Each  allegation  of  sexual  harassment  and  other misconduct which may contribute to an offensive, hostile  or  intimidating  work  environment  should  be  reported as soon as possible after the incident occurs. There is no specific time requirement for employees to report  instances  of  sexual  harassment  under  the  accountability board process. However, the city's ability to deal with such issues appropriately and effectively, particularly when disciplinary action is warranted, is greatly diminished if  the allegations are not reported timely. Accordingly, employees are encouraged to report  such  incidents  promptly.  The  goal  is  that  such allegations will be reported to the accountability board and, if  appropriate, investigated and appropriate action initiated within a total of fifty (50) workdays from the date the allegation was reported. Specific timeframes for various stages of the process are provided for in this
division. Extensions of  timeframes prescribed by this division shall be within the discretion of the accountability board chairperson.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.70; Ord. No. 01-2, § 5, 2-14-2001)

Sec.  2-570.72.  Definitions/responsibilities.
(a)  Accountability board. The accountability board oversees  the  processing  of  all  allegations  of  sexual harassment and other misconduct which may contribute to an offensive, hostile or intimidating work environment to ensure that city officials are accountable for properly responding to such allegations. The accountability board will ensure that allegations are resolved timely,  handled  consistently  throughout  the  agency, and appropriately resolved. The accountability board tracks and monitors all allegations and their outcomes and seeks to identify trends in such allegations and the manner in which they are resolved. Based on analyses of  data  collected,  the  accountability  board  recommends  policies  and  procedures  to  correct  identified systemic problems in city policies and practices. The accountability board will continually evaluate the procedures set forth in this division and their effectiveness.
(b)  Accountability board chairperson. The accountability board chairperson directs the proceedings of the accountability board and provides the city commission and city manager with a report of  the accountability board's activities on a quarterly basis. The accountability board chairperson resolves any conflicts of interests involving  members  of  the  accountability  board  and makes decisions concerning issues of scope and timeliness raised during the processing of  allegations. The accountability board chairperson may alter these procedures as needed to ensure the best interests of  the agency are satisfied.
CD2:94
ADMINISTRATION
(c)  Accountability board coordinator. The accountability board coordinator organizes the administrative activities of the accountability board. The coordinator tracks the progress of  individual cases, schedules accountability board meetings, and dockets reported cases for review by the accountability board. The coordinator  notifies  affected  personnel  to  ensure  their  attendance at accountability board meetings. The coordinator consults with managers and supervisors involved in the process. The accountability board coordinator shall be a designated person from the city's department of human resources.
(d)  Complaining  party.  The  complaining  party  is any individual alleging sexual harassment, misconduct of a sexual nature, or reprisal or retaliation for reporting allegations or cooperating in the inquiry or investigation of such allegations, whether as the person against whom such conduct is directed or as a witness to such conduct.
(e)  Respondent.  The  respondent  is  an  individual against whom an allegation is made.
(f)  Accountable  official.  The  accountable  official shall be the city manager, or his designee, is responsible for ensuring appropriate and timely processing of allegations within the city in accordance with these procedures. The accountable official may designate subordinate manager to interview the complaining party, advise the respondent, and perform supervisory duties relative to any appropriate action required. Depending on the position of the respondent, there may be instances in  which  the  accountable  official  himself  or  herself must perform the supervisory duties relative to appropriate action.
(g)  Human  resources  specialist.  The  human  resource  (HR)  specialist  designated  for  accountability board  matters  advises  supervisors  and  management officials on policies and procedures applicable to allegations covered by this division.
(h)  Investigator. The investigator conducts a formal investigation to determine facts relevant to allegations of  sexual harassment or misconduct which may contribute  to  an  offensive,  hostile  or  intimidating  work environment and, on completion, provides a written report of investigation (ROI).
(i)  The  term  "day"  refers  to  administrative  workdays. (Code 1983, § 2-570.72; Ord. No. 01-2, § 7, 2-14-2001)

Sec.  2-570.73.  Procedures.
(a) Introduction.
(1) The procedures prescribed below apply to all allegations of sexual harassment and misconduct  which  may  contribute  to  an  offensive, hostile or intimidating work environment, regardless  of  where  they  originate  within  the city.  In  some  cases,  allegations  may  be  reported by the complaining party to a supervisor  within  the  city.  While  employees  are  encouraged to report sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct to their managers or supervisors, this may not always be feasible. Accordingly, allegations may come to light through the department of human resources or an EEO officer. Allegations that become known through these sources will be reported to the accountability board.
(2) Allegations of sexual harassment and misconduct or reprisal for reporting such allegations or for cooperating in an inquiry or investigation related to such allegations, regardless of where they originate, must be reported to the accountability board coordinator within two (2) workdays of the date the allegation is first made.
(b) Phase I-Report of allegation.
(1) Whenever sexual harassment, or other misconduct, is alleged by a city employee to a supervisory or managerial official, the accountable official  must report the allegation to the accountability board coordinator within two (2) workdays  of  the  date  the  allegation  is  first made.  When  the  allegation  is  reported  to  a supervisor or manager other than the accountable official, that manager or supervisor must immediately notify the appropriate accountable  official  to  ensure  the  two  (2)  day  time requirement  is  met.  When  reporting  to  the accountability board coordinator, the accountable  official  shall  provide  as  much  pertinent information as is known at that time, without additional inquiry. At a minimum, the identities  of  the  respondent  and  the  complaining party should be provided. Reporting is done verbally by telephone or facsimile.

§ 2-570.73

(2) When  an  allegation  or  complaint  of  sexual harassment or other  misconduct  is  made  to the EEO officer, the EEO officer is responsible for reporting the allegation to the accountability  board  coordinator  within  two  (2)  workdays. If  anonymity is requested by the complainant during the informal counseling period, the facts of  the allegation will be referred to the accountability board in a manner that does not reveal the complaining party's identity.
(3) If an allegation brought to the accountability board's  attention  by  means  of  the  EEO  is specific enough to allow management action, the accountability board coordinator shall notify the accountable official. If  an allegation received from an anonymous or confidential source is too vague to support continued inquiry,  the  accountability  board  shall  document the allegation, but will take no further action. The accountability board will not initiate investigation for vague or undefined allegations. In addition, the ability of the accountability board to investigate and take appropriate action  may  be  limited  when  allegations  are anonymous and/or confidential.
(4) Allegations reported to the department of human resources must be reported to the accountability board coordinator within two (2) workdays of the date the allegation is first made.
(5) If a manager or supervisor receives an allegation of sexual harassment that involves a contractor, he or she should immediately contact the accountability board coordinator, who will notify the appropriate contracting officer.
(6) Upon receipt of an allegation, the accountability board coordinator shall ensure the allegation and all pertinent facts are brought to the accountability board's attention. In those cases, reported by sources other than the accountable official, the coordinator will also ensure that the accountable official is notified of the allegation.  Based  on  the  information  provided, and in consultation with the accountable official,  an  initial  determination  will  be made by the  accountability  board  as  to  the appropriate  manner  in  which  to  handle  the allegation.
CD2:96
(7) Reporting the allegation to the accountability board in no way impacts the processing of an EEO complaint concerning the same matter. The accountability board process does not extend  or  limit  the  timeframes  in  the  EEO  or grievance processes. Allegations of sexual harassment  pursued  through  the  EEO  process will  be  handled  in  accordance with the laws governing the filing and handling of claims as provided for by the equal employment opportunity commission.
(c) Phase II-Initial steps. After reporting the allegation to the board, or receiving the allegation from the board coordinator, the accountable official has several responsibilities  that  must  be  accomplished  virtually simultaneously or in rapid sequence.
(1) Initial interview. The accountable official shall consult with the designated HR point of contact in determining the appropriate person in the city to conduct the initial interview of the complaining  party.  Normally,  this  will  be  a manager or supervisor who has not been alleged, in any way, to be personally involved in the allegation of sexual harassment or misconduct. Under unusual circumstances, such as a case of particular sensitivity, or a complaining party who requires special assistance, the accountable official may determine that someone from outside the city should conduct the interview.
a. The purpose of the initial interview is to determine, to the extent possible, the nature of the conduct leading to the allegation and to identify the parties involved.
b. The  person  designated  to  conduct  the interview  shall  consult  with  the  designated HR point of contact for guidance on  how  to  conduct  the  interview.  Responding  to  the  person  designated  to conduct the initial interview shall be a priority for the HR specialist and shall be accomplished within one (1) workday of contact.
c. The person conducting the initial interview shall request that the complaining party  provide  a  written  statement  that describes  in  his  or  her  own  words  as many  details  of  the  alleged  behavior/

text:
Sec.  2-570.74.  Cases involving noncity personnel.
Allegations of sexual harassment, or other misconduct of a sexual nature, by or against persons who are not city employees will also be reviewed by the accountability board. If the respondent is a city employee, the procedures described in section 2-570.73 of  this division apply in their entirety. In cases in which the individual against whom the allegation is made is not a city employee, the allegation will be reported to the cognizant contracting officer for referral to the contractor or to the individual's parent organization, as appropriate, for coordination in conducting any inquiry or investigation or in resolving the allegation. The accountability board will track and monitor these allegations to ensure timely and appropriate action.
(Code 1983, § 2-570.74; Ord. No. 01-2, § 9, 2-14-2001)

text:
Sec.  2-570.81.  Created;  composition;  term  of  office; qualifications;  organization;  meetings; records.
A historic environmental preservation board ("board") is hereby created, which shall be an advisory body to the commission, consisting of  five (5) members,  each  of  whom  shall  be  appointed  by  the  city commission, for a term of  four (4) years. The board shall  also  consist  of  two  (2)  alternate  members  appointed  by  the  city  commission.  Alternate  members shall serve a term of two (2) years. An alternate member  shall  replace  a  regular  member  when  a  regular member is unavailable to attend a meeting. Each member of the board shall serve until the expiration of his or her term. Members shall be eligible for reappointment. The city commission shall attempt to appoint architects, realtors, historians, art historians, lawyers, engineers, archaeologists or other individuals from the business, financial, or other segments of  the community who, by virtue of their profession or business, have demonstrated  concern  for  historic  preservation.  The historic  environmental  preservation  board  shall  include not less than one (1) architect; one (1) real estate agent  or  attorney  at  law;  and  one  (1)  historian  or architectural historian. The city manager shall provide qualified professional staff for the board.
(a) At least three (3) members of the historic environmental  board  shall  be  residents  of  the city.  The  city  commission,  within  its  discre-
CD2:99
§ 2-570.81
OPA-LOCKA CODE
tion, may appoint up to a maximum of two (2) members of the board who are not residents of the city. These two (2) appointments shall be made  on  the  basis  of  civic  pride,  integrity, experience and interest in the field of historic preservation and city beautification. Members of  the  historic  environmental  preservation board shall hold no other public office or position in the city.
(b) The  members  of  the  historic  environmental preservation board shall elect a chair and vice chair from among its appointed members. The city  commission  may  remove  members  and vacancies shall be filled for the unexpired term of any removed member.
(c) Meetings of  the historic environmental preservation board shall meet not less than six (6) times in any calendar year. Records shall be maintained pursuant to state law, findings and determinations showing the vote on each matter and shall file the record and approved minutes of each meeting with the city clerk within thirty (30) days of the date of the meeting, or as soon thereafter as practicable. Members of the  historic  environmental  board  shall  serve without compensation.
(d) The historic environmental preservation board may adopt reasonable rules of  procedure to govern  the  conduct  of  its  business  and  the holding  of  public  hearings  and  workshops, consistent  with  procedures  established  for  it by the city commission.

text:
Sec.  2-570.82.  Duties and responsibilities.
The historical preservation board shall have the following enumerated powers and duties:
(1) Adopt  or  amend  rules  of  procedure  for  its meetings.
(2) Advise the city commission as to designated individual  sites,  districts  and  archeological zones.
(3) Recommend the issuance or denial of certificates  of  appropriateness  and  certificates  to dig.
Supp. No. 1
CD2:100
(4) Recommend the approval of historical markers and recommend the issuance of certificates of  recognition for individual sites and designated properties in a district.
(5) Recommend zoning and building code amendments to the proper authorities.
(6) Recommend to the city commission guidelines for  preservation  and  criteria  for  issuance  by staff of regular certificates of appropriateness.
(7) Promote the awareness of  historic  preservation and its community benefits.
(8) No actions of this board will supersede or be construed as superseding the authority of the city commission.
(9) Review  and  recommend  update  the  historic survey  as  it  applies  to  the  city  and  conduct such local research as is considered appropriate.
(10) Implement the authority of  this division and fulfill the tasks set forth for this board by the city commissioners.
(11) Record and maintain records of  the board's actions and decisions.
(12) Follow and abide by the laws of  the United States of  America, the state, county, and the city.
(13) Provide an annual report to the city commission.

text:
Sec.  2-570.83.  Scope of regulations.
This division is intended to and shall govern and be applicable to all property located in the city. Nothing contained herein shall be deemed to supersede or conflict with applicable building and zoning codes. Provisions contained herein shall be cumulative and read in conjunction with other laws, rules and regulations. It is the legislative intent of  the city commission that this division shall meet the requirements of  chapter 16A, section 16A-3.1 of Miami-Dade County Code of Ordinances as a qualified municipal historic preservation ordinance, and that this division shall be filed with the clerk of  Miami-Dade County board of  county commissioners and with the national register of historical places for certification to be eligible under the relevant Tax Act.
(Ord. No. 2022-02, § 2(2-570.83), 1-12-2022)

text:
Sec.  2-570.84.  Definitions.
The following words, terms and phrases, when used in  this  division,  shall  have  the  meanings  ascribed  to them in this section, except where the context clearly indicates a different meaning:
(1) Archeological zone means an area designated by this ordinance which likely to yield information on the history and pre-history of the city based on prehistoric settlement  patterns  in  the  city  as  determined  by  the results of  the Dade County historic survey and local research. These zones will tend to conform to natural physiographic features which were the focal points for prehistoric and historic activities.
(2) Certificates of appropriateness means a certificate issued by the city commission after rec-
Supp. No. 1
§ 2-570.84
ommendation by the board permitting certain alterations  or  improvements  to  a  designated property.
(A) Regular certificate of appropriateness. A regular certificate of appropriateness shall be issued and approved by the city manager through the administrative review process based on the guidelines of minor repair and renovation projects.
(B) Special certificate of appropriateness. For all applications for a special certificate of appropriateness  involving  the  demolition, removal, reconstruction or new construction  at  an  individual  site  or  in  a district a special certificate of appropriateness is required that is issued directly by the board.
(3) Certificate to dig means a certificate that gives the board's permission for certain digging projects that may involve the discovery of as yet unknown or known archeological sites in an archeological zone. This certificate  is  issued  by  staff  of  the  board  based  on  the guidelines for preservation approved by the board.
(4) Certificate of recognition means a certificate issued  by  the  board  recognizing  properties  designated pursuant to this division.
(5) City commission means the City of  Opa-locka Commission.
(6) Demolition means the complete constructive removal of a building of any site.
(7) Districts means  a  collection  of  archeological sites, buildings, structures, landscape features or other improvements that are concentrated in the same area and have been designated as a district pursuant to this ordinance.
(8) Exterior means all outside surfaces of a building or structure.
(9) Guidelines for preservation means criteria used by staff in determining the validity of applications for a regular certificate of  appropriateness and any certificate to dig and to establish a set of guide- lines for the preservation of buildings in the city. Minimum guidelines for preservation shall be that of  the Secretary of Interior's Standards for the treatment of historic properties, as may be amended from time to time. The city commission may establish additional standards.
CD2:101
§ 2-570.84
OPA-LOCKA CODE
(10) Historical preservation board means the board created and established by this ordinance as described in section 2-570.81.
(11) Historic survey means a comprehensive survey compiled by the historic preservation division of  the Miami-Dade County Office of Community and Economic  Development  involving  the  identification,  research and documentation of buildings, sites and structures  of any  historical,  cultural,  archeological  or architectural, importance in Miami-Dade County, Florida.
(12) Individual site means an archeological site, building,  structure,  place  or  other  improvement  that  has been designated as an individual site pursuant to this division. Under the provisions of this division, interior spaces may be regulated only where a building or structure is designated individual site.
(13) National  register  of  historic  places means  a federal listing maintained by the U.S. Department of the Interior of buildings, sites, structures and districts that have attained a quality of  significance as determined  by  the  Historic  Preservation  Act  of  1966  as amended.
(14) Ordinary repairs  or  maintenance means work done to prevent deterioration of a building or structure or decay of or damage to a building or structure or any part thereof by re- storing the building or structure as nearly  as  practicable  to  its  condition  prior  to  such deterioration, decay or damage.
(15) Owner of  a designated property means as reflected on the current Metropolitan Dade County tax rolls or current title holder.
(16) Qualified staff may be considered outside contractors of  the city and shall be a person who has a bachelor's degree in historic preservation, architecture, architectural history, history, or other closely related field,  and who has at least three (3) years of  professional experience in the field of historic preservation or as a historic preservation planner; or who has a master's degree in the above mentioned fields and who has at least one (1) year of  professional experience in the field of historic preservation or as a historic preservation planner.
Supp. No. 1
CD2:102
(17) Landscape feature means any improvement or vegetation,, including, but not limited to outbuildings, walls,  courtyards,  fences,  shrubbery,  trees  sidewalks, planters, plantings, gates, street furniture and exterior lighting.
(18) Historic designated property means any property listed on the City of Opa-locka Historic Register or contributing property within the designated historic district.
(19) Minor repair or renovation project means any alteration to an exterior of historic designated property that  is  considered  to  be  of  minimal  impact  on  the property's historic character, such as routine maintenance,  replacement  of  like-for-like  materials,  minor paint color changes, or minor repairs to windows and doors, as further defined in the COA Matrix.
The definitions set forth in the Miami-Dade County Ordinance No. 81-13, chapter 16-A pertaining to historic preservation shall by adopted and also apply to this section in the event of  conflict and as may other-
wise be amended from time to time. (Ord. No. 2022-02, § 2(2-570.84), 1-12-2022; Ord. No.
2025-08, § 2, 4-9-2025)

Administrative  approval  process  for  minor  repair and renovation projects:

(b) Review by zoning, planning and community development. The  director  and  the  designated staff shall review the application to determine
ADMINISTRATION
if  the  project  qualifies  as  a  minor  repair  or renovation  project.  If  approved,  the  zoning, planning  and  community  development  shall issue a certificate of  appropriateness without further review by the HEPB.
(c) Notification. The applicant shall be required to notify any adjacent property owners of the administrative approval of  a minor repair or renovation project.
(d) Conditions for administrative approval. All minor repair or renovation projects must comply with the established City of  Opa-locka Historic Preservation Design Guidelines.

text:
Sec.  2-570.87.  Designation process and procedure.
I.  The city commission shall have the authority to designate areas, places, buildings, structures, landscape features, archeological sites and other improvements or physical features, as individual sites, districts, or archeological zones that are significant in the city's history, architecture, archeology, or culture and possesses an integrity of  location, design, setting, materials, workmanship or association, or:
(A) Are associated with distinctive elements of the cultural, social political, economic, scientific, religious, prehistoric and architectural history that have contributed to the pattern of history in the community, Miami-Dade County, South Florida, the state or the nation;
(B) Are associated with the lives of persons significant in our past;
(C) Embody  the  distinctive  characteristics  of  a type, period, style or method of construction or  work  of  a  master;  or  that  possess  high artistic value, or that represent a distinguishable entity whose components may lack individual distinction;
Supp. No. 1
CD2:102.1
§ 2-570.87
ADMINISTRATION
(D) Have yielded, or are likely to yield information in history or prehistory; or
(E) Are listed in the national register of  historic places.  The city commission shall conduct a separate public hearing to consider for designation  each  property  within  its  jurisdiction listed in the national register of historic places;
II.  Certain properties which include cemeteries, birthplaces,  properties  owned  by  religious  institutions,  or used for religious purposes, structures that have been moved from their original locations, properties commemorative in nature and properties that have achieved significance within the last twenty-five years, will not normally be considered for designation. However, such properties  will  qualify  if  they  are  integral  parts  of districts that do meet the criteria, or if they fall within the following categories:
(A) A religious property deriving primary significance from architectural or artistic distinction of historical importance.
(B) A building or structure removed from its location but which is primarily significant for architectural value, or is the surviving structure most importantly associated with an historic event or person.
(C) A birthplace or grave of an historical figure of outstanding  importance  if  there  is  no  other appropriate site or building directly associated with his/her productive life.
(D) A cemetery which derives its primary significance from graves of persons of transcendent importance, from age, distinctive design features, or from association with historic events.
(E) A property  primarily  commemorative  in  intent if design, age, tradition, or symbolic value has invested it with its own historical significance.
(F) A property or district achieving significance within the past twenty-five (25) years if it is of exceptional importance.
III.  Prior to the designation of an individual site, a district, or an archeological zone, an investigation and designation report must be filed with city. The format of  these  reports  may  vary  according  to  the  type  of designation, however all reports must address the following: The historical, cultural, architectural, and ar-
CD2:103
§ 2-570.87
cheological significance of  the property of  properties being recommended for designation; a recommendation of boundaries for districts and archeological zones and  identification  of  boundaries  of  individual  sites being designated; a recommendation of  standards to be adopted by the city commission in carrying out its regulatory function under this ordinance with respect to  certificates  of  appropriateness  and  certificates  to dig. Where a report is filed recommending designation of a district, the report must identify those properties, if  any, within the district which are not historically or architecturally compatible with structures in the district. The standards for regulating such nonconforming properties shall provide that a certificate of appropriateness may be required only for new construction on such properties. All reports shall take into consideration projected, proposed or existing public improvements and developmental or renewal plans.
